episode.throughLine: A woman told a friend why she doubted she could attend another college, worked toward it, and sought encouragement when money and missing preparation nearly stopped her.

contentProfile.contentNote: Financial pressure, interrupted education and doubt about belonging, with practical support from friends and a teacher.

facts.statement: Hurston was born January 7, 1891, attended Morgan Academy from September 1917 to June 1918, attended Howard Prep in 1918-19, and entered Howard University in 1919. The memoir puts the college-choice conversation before the summer move from Morgan; about twenty-seven is an approximate age, not a verified month for the conversation.

As Hurston considered college she planned to remain at Morgan. Mae Miller visited her cousins Bernice and Gwendolyn Hughes for a weekend; Hurston joined them. After several hours of fun, Miller told Hurston she belonged at Howard and asked her to come.

sourceRefs.locator: IX School Again, paragraph beginning 'When it came time to consider college'

facts.statement: Hurston had heard about Howard's fashionable fraternities, sororities and clothes and believed she could not make it there.

sourceRefs.locator: IX, paragraph beginning 'I had heard all about the swank fraternities'

facts.statement: Hurston told Mae Miller that she believed she could not make it at Howard.

sourceRefs.locator: IX, same 'I had heard all about' paragraph, final sentence

facts.statement: Bernice Hughes offered Hurston a place in her family's home without room or board costs and said they would help find a job to pay tuition.

sourceRefs.locator: IX, paragraph beginning 'You can come and live at our house'

facts.statement: That summer Hurston moved to Washington, worked first as a waitress and then as a manicurist, gathered her first quarter's tuition, and went to register.

sourceRefs.locator: IX, paragraph beginning 'So that summer I moved on to Washington'

facts.statement: At Howard Hurston remained short of money and faced trouble because Morgan did not then have a class-A rating. She was about to give up when she talked with Dwight Holmes, her former night-school teacher; she subsequently completed the missing hours.

sourceRefs.locator: IX, paragraph beginning 'Lo and behold, there was Dwight Holmes', together with Holmes's night-school identification at 'There I met the man' earlier in chapter IX

facts.statement: Holmes encouraged Hurston as much as he could; she stayed and completed the required additional work.

sourceRefs.locator: IX, 'Lo and behold' paragraph, final sentence

facts.statement: At her first college assembly Hurston sat in the chapel, felt accepted into the university and inwardly pledged not to make it ashamed of her.

sourceRefs.locator: IX, paragraph beginning 'I shall never forget my first college assembly'

facts.statement: Zora Neale Hurston wrote the novel Their Eyes Were Watching God.
Hurston died in 1960 with too little money for her own funeral; neighbors collected funds and her grave was initially unmarked.

sourceRefs.locator: Biography, death and burial paragraphs before Alice Walker's search

arc.canonicalText: She was with two school friends and their visiting cousin. She was about twenty-seven. In her memory, they had spent a few hours having fun. The cousin had come for the weekend. She planned to stay at her present school for college. But the visitor thought she belonged at another college. She asked her to come.
arc.sourceNote: One remembered weekend encounter at Morgan, before the summer 1918 move. No room, furnishings, pastime, gesture or additional motive is invented. The approximate age combines the estate chronology with the memoir's ordered college-choice/summer-move sequence.

arc.canonicalText: She did not believe she could manage at the college her visitor had suggested. She had heard about its student clubs and their fine clothes. She did not think she could make it there.
arc.sourceNote: The doubt is Hurston's explicitly stated belief at the invitation, not the earlier anticipated fear of a dean. Clothing and clubs are the source's particulars; the prose does not turn class anxiety into actual rejection. This is a spare low point, not a newly invented crisis.

arc.canonicalText: She told her friend's cousin that she did not think she could manage there. She put that doubt into words.
arc.sourceNote: The small act is telling Mae, not becoming confident or being rescued. The memoir supplies only that brief statement, so no dialogue or expanded explanation is manufactured. Practical help belongs to the following compression.

arc.canonicalText: One of her school friends offered a place in her family's home. She also offered to help find work to cover tuition. That summer the young woman moved to the other city. She worked first as a waitress, then doing customers' nails. She gathered enough for the first term and went to register. But her savings had not removed the difficulty. She was still short of money. Her previous school's standing was another problem. There was more preparatory work to do. At registration, she came close to giving up. The first term's money was not enough.
arc.sourceNote: Chronological compression from the weekend offer through summer work and registration. The real failed sufficiency is that savings and prior schooling do not settle admission needs; no failed examination, missing paycheck or invented practice failure is asserted. The memoir's accreditation wording is kept distinct from any guessed subject or exact missing-credit count.

arc.canonicalText: At the new school, she talked with her former night-school teacher. He was there too. She was almost ready to give up. He encouraged her as much as he could. She stayed.
arc.sourceNote: One remembered conversation, not a fictional registration-desk speech. The memoir directly connects Holmes's encouragement with her staying; its actual wording is not provided and none is invented. The event is very briefly documented, so the passage stays sparse. Completion of the work is deferred to became.

arc.canonicalText: She completed the missing schoolwork. A year of preparatory study came before she entered college. At her first college assembly, she sat in the chapel and felt taken in. She wanted never to make the school ashamed of her. She had finished the preparatory work, not college. More classes lay ahead.
arc.sourceNote: Ends at first college entry in 1919. The memoir's undated work schedule and repeated assembly particulars are not assigned to that first assembly or silently dated inside this narrow episode. Her remembered inward pledge is paraphrased without quotation marks. No lifetime achievement list or claim that money problems were permanently solved.

arc.canonicalText:
Her name was Zora Neale Hurston.

She wrote the novel Their Eyes Were Watching God. Your life is not theirs. But a piece of this story may still sit beside you. You are allowed to want something you have wanted for a long time. You do not have to be early.
arc.sourceNote: Name and title appear only here. The reader lines offer no instruction or prediction.

dramatizationLimits: Do not invent a room, gesture, exact dialogue or private realization in the weekend invitation or Holmes conversation.
Retrospective memoir particulars remain probable; corrected age and educational chronology come from the estate chronology.
Do not make practical help an instant end to financial pressure or evidence that one person caused Hurston's career.
avoidRules: Keep names, calendar years, cities and institutions anonymous until the bridge.
Do not repeat the memoir's altered age or two-year Morgan duration as settled chronology.
Do not transform concern about social class into actual exclusion or cruelty by classmates.
Do not move the Morgan friendship turn after Howard registration.
Do not add surgery or undated later university routines to this 1917-19 episode envelope.
